εὐτελὴς γὰρ αὕτη ἡ καύχησις ὅπου πάντα ἐστὶν ὑμῶν, καὶ οἱ ἀπόστολοι–διὰ γὰρ τοὺς
ὠφελουμένους ἀπεστάλησαν–, καὶ ὁ κόσμος ὑμῶν δι' οὓς γέγονε πρὸς ἀπόλαυσιν,
καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ὑμῶν ὡς σωζομένων, καὶ ὁ θάνατος– εἰ μὴ γὰρ ἦν τὰ τοῦ θανάτου φοβερά,
οὐκ ἂν τὰ τῆς μελλούσης ζωῆς προετιμήθη–· κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν γὰρ λόγον εἴρηται τὰ
ἐνεστῶτα καὶ μέλλοντα· οἱ γὰρ τῶν ἐνεστώτων καταφρονοῦντες ὡς προσκαίρων
τῶν μελλόντων ἐπιτυγχάνουσιν. πάντα οὖν τὰ προειρημένα ὑμῶν, ὅτι καὶ ὑμεῖς
Χριστοῦ γεγόνατε, καὶ οἱ τῷ Χριστῷ προσοικειώμενοι ἀρέσκονται θεῷ. Πάντα ὑφ'
ὑμῶν. πῶς καὶ τίνα τρόπον; ὅτι καὶ ὑμεῖς Χριστοῦ γεγόνατε, καὶ ἵνα δείξῃ ὅτι οἱ τῷ
Χριστῷ προσοικειώμενοι ἀρέσκονται θεῷ, ἐπήγαγεν· Χριστὸς δὲ θεοῦ. 1 Kor 4,1Ἀρκεῖ
μὲν ἡμῖν τὸ ὡς ὑπηρέτας Χριστοῦ τιμᾶσθαι, τὸ δὲ ἀφ' ἡμῶν τινας ὀνομάζεσθαι
φορτικόν. 1 Kor 4,2Ὑμεῖς μὲν ὡς ὑπηρέτας θεοῦ ὁρᾶτε ἡμᾶς, τίς δὲ ὑπηρέτης πιστός,
μὴ ὑμεῖς ζητεῖτε–τοῦτο γὰρ ἐν ὑμῖν κινδυνεύεται–καὶ οὔτε ἄξιον τοὺς διδασκάλους
κρίνεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν μαθητῶν. διὰ τί δὲ ταῦτά φησιν; ἐπειδὴ συνεῖδέν τινας μὲν τῶν
διδασκάλων ἀναξίους τιμωμένους ὑπ' αὐτῶν, τοὺς δὲ ἀξίους περιορωμένους, ὅθεν
καὶ προεώρα σχίσματα ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐσόμενα. διὸ καὶ σφοδρότερον ἐγκαλεῖ σπεύδων
καταστεῖλαι τὸ πάθος. 1 Kor 4,3Ἵνα δὲ μὴ δόξῃ ὡς καταφρονηθεὶς ὑπερόπτως ταῦτα
λέγειν, μονονουχὶ τοῦτο λέγει· μὴ νομίσητε ταῦτά με ὑπὲρ ἐμαυτοῦ ἀποστέλλειν· οὐ
γὰρ οὕτω πολιτεύομαι ἵνα ὑφ' ὑμῶν ἀνακριθῶ· ἀνάξιον γὰρ τοῦτο ἡγοῦμαι ὡς πρὸς
ὑμᾶς καὶ πάντα ἄνθρωπον. ἀνθρωπίνην 239 δὲ ἡμέραν τὸν ἄνθρωπον καλεῖ, τὸ
πρόσκαιρον καὶ ἐφήμερον τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ζωῆς δηλῶν. εἶτα ἐπειδὴ μέγα δοκεῖ
εἶναι τὸ εἰπεῖν οὐδὲν ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα, ἐπήγαγεν ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ δεδικαίωμαι·
ἔστι γὰρ κατ' ἄγνοιαν πταίσαντα μὴ πλήττεσθαι τὸ συνειδός. ἔπειτα οὐ τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν
φαῦλον δικαιοῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸ κατορθοῦν ἀρετὴν τελειοῖ. εἰκὸς δὲ ὅτι καὶ μετριοπαθῶν
εἶπεν τοῦτο· μὴ οὖν φρονεῖτε μείζονα ἢ καθ' ὑμᾶς, ἀλλ' ἀναμένετε τὸν κριτήν. 1 Kor
4,5 ∆ι' ὅλου ἔχεται τοῦ σκοποῦ σωφρονίζων τοὺς βουλομένους ἀπὸ μὲν τοῦ δεῖνος
ὀνομάζεσθαι, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ δεῖνος μὴ ὀνομάζεσθαι· τοῦτο γὰρ κρινόντων ἐστὶν τόν τε
ἄξιον καὶ μὴ ἄξιον. μὴ οὖν φρονεῖτε μείζονα ἢ καθ' ὑμᾶς, ἀλλ' ἀναμένετε τὸν
κριτήν· ὑμᾶς μὲν γὰρ καὶ πεπλασμένον ἦθος ἀπατᾶν ἐγχωρεῖ, τὸν δὲ φωτίζοντα τὰ
κρυπτὰ τοῦ σκότους οὐκ ἄν τι τῶν κεκρυμμένων διαλάθοι. ταῦτα δὲ εἶπεν, ὡς ὅτι
πολλὰ παρ' αὐτοῖς κατ' ἀπάτην ἐγίνετο καὶ ἀνάξιοι ἐτιμῶντο. Οἱ τιμώμενοι οὐ
πάντως ἦσαν καλοί, ἀλλ' ἕως σχήματος ἐπεῖχον τὴν ἀρετήν, παρεωρῶντο δὲ οἱ
φύσει καλοί· οὐ γὰρ ἂν ταῦτα εἶπεν. 1 Kor 4,6 Ἑαυτὸν καὶἈπολλῶ παράγει σιωπήσας
τὰ πρόσωπα τῶν ἀπαιτούντων τιμᾶσθαι καὶ ἀπ' αὐτῶν ὀνομάζεσθαι τοὺς μαθητάς,
ἵνα τύπον καὶ ἀκολουθίαν ἀφ' ἡμῶν λάβητε μετρίως προσφέρεσθαι τοῖς
διδασκάλοις. καὶ μὴ ὑπὲρ ἃ γέγραπται φρονεῖτε περὶ ἡμῶν, ἀλλὰ λογίζεσθε ἡμᾶς
ὑπηρέτας Χριστοῦ καὶ οἰκονόμους μυστηρίων θεοῦ, καὶ μὴ τοὺς μὲν τῶν
διδασκάλων ἀτιμάζετε, τοὺς δὲ τιμᾶτε. Σαφέστερον ἐν τούτοις ἤλεγξεν αὐτῶν τὴν
γνώμην· ὁ γὰρ ὀνομαζόμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ δεῖνος, τὸν δεῖνα δὲ περιορῶν, ὑπὲρ ἐκείνου
μὲν ἐφυσιοῦτο, κατ' ἐκείνου δὲ εἶχεν τὴν φυσίωσιν. 1 Kor 4,7 Σὲ τὸν βουλόμενον
ἀπὸ τοῦδε καλεῖσθαι ἢ τόνδε καταλιμπάνειν, τίς διακρίνει; οὐχὶ ἀναμένεις τὸν
κριτήν; σὺ ὁ ὑπακούων ἀνα240 μένεις τὸν κριτήν, καὶ τὸν διδάσκαλον τῇ σῇ κρίσει
ὑποβάλλεις; 239,ξολ2 Σὲ τὸν λαϊκὸν τίς διακρίνει ἐφ' οἷς ἢ φρονεῖς ἢ πράττεις, ὅτι σὺ
ἑτέρους διακρίνειν τολμᾷς, καὶ ταῦτα διδασκάλους; οὐχὶ ὁ κύριος; 240,ξολ2 εἰ οὖν σὺ
ὁ μαθητὴς τὸν κύριον ἀναμένεις κριτήν, πῶς τὸν διδάσκαλον τῇ σῇ ὑποβάλλεις
κρίσει, τὸν μὲν ἄξιον λέγων, τὸν δὲ ἀνάξιον; ∆ιὰ τί νομίζεις ἔχειν πλεονέκτημα ὃ
μήτε ἔχεις μήτε εἴληφας; λέγει δὲ τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν σύνεσιν δι' ἧς καὶ δυνατὸν
καὶ διδασκάλους κρίνειν καὶ δοκιμάζειν. Εἰ καὶ ἔλαβες τὴν σύνεσιν ἀπὸ θεοῦ, δεῖ τῷ
θεῷ τῷ δεδωκότι αὐτὴν δόξαν προσάγειν, οὐ μὴν ἐπὶ σαυτῷ μέγα φρονεῖν καὶ
ἐπαίρεσθαι ὡς οἰκεῖον προβαλλόμενον πλεονέκτημα. 1 Kor 4,8 Οὐχ ὅτι οὕτως εἶχε τὰ
κατ' αὐτούς, ἀλλὰ δείκνυσιν ὅτι οὕτω διέκειντο ψευδῆ περὶ ἑαυτῶν δοξάζοντες, καὶ
ᾤοντο πάσης πεπληρῶσθαι γνώσεως ὡς λοιπὸν καὶ διδασκάλους κρίνειν. ἤδη
προσKorῆ γέγονεν ὑμῖν τὰ χαρίσματα καὶ οὐκ ἀεὶ ποθητά. τὸ δὲ χωρὶς ἡμῶν δηλοῖ
μηδέπω βασιλευσάντων ὑμεῖς ἔφθητε βασιλεῦσαι, τὸ δὲ καὶ ὄφελόν γε διὰ μέσου
pass_a_gloss: (Continuing: he teaches them not to boast over wise men either;) for cheap is this boasting where all things are yours: both the apostles - for they were sent for the sake of those being helped - and the world (is) yours, for whose sake it came to be for enjoyment, and life (is) yours as (people) being saved, and death - for if the things of death were not fearful, the things of the coming life would not have been preferred -; for according to the same reasoning the present and coming things are said: for those who despise the present things as temporary obtain the coming things. So all the things said before (are) yours, because you also have become Christ's, and those made Christ's own please God. 'All things by (read: of) you.' How and in what manner? Because you also have become Christ's; and in order to show that those made Christ's own please God, he added: 'and Christ (is) God's'. [Label 1 Cor 4:1.] It is enough for us to be honoured as servants of Christ, but (for) some to be named from us (is) burdensome. [Label 1 Cor 4:2.] You see us as servants of God, but who (is) a faithful servant, do not you seek - for this is endangered among you - and it is not worthy for the teachers to be judged by the disciples. And why does he say these things? Since he perceived that some of the teachers, unworthy, were honoured by them, but the worthy overlooked, from which he also foresaw schisms that would be among them. Therefore he also accuses more vehemently, hastening to put down the passion. [Label 1 Cor 4:3.] So that he may not seem, as despised, to say these things haughtily, he all but says this: do not think that I send these things on my own behalf; for I do not so conduct myself that I be examined by you; for I consider this unworthy as regards you and every man. [page 239] He calls man 'human day', showing the temporary and ephemeral (nature) of the life of men. Then since it seems a great thing to say 'I know nothing with myself', he added 'but I am not justified in this'; for it is (possible) for one who stumbled through ignorance not to be struck in the conscience. Then, not doing a bad thing does not justify, but accomplishing virtue perfects. And it is likely that he said this also being moderate: so do not think greater than (befits) you, but wait for the judge. [Label 1 Cor 4:5.] Throughout he holds to the aim, bringing to sobriety those wishing to be named from so-and-so and not to be named from so-and-so; for this is (the part) of those judging the worthy and the unworthy. So do not think greater than (befits) you, but wait for the judge: for even a feigned character can deceive you, but nothing of the hidden things could escape the one who illuminates the hidden things of darkness. And he said these things as (because) many things among them happened by deceit and unworthy (men) were honoured. Those honoured were not altogether good, but held virtue as far as appearance, and those good by nature were overlooked; for (otherwise) he would not have said these things. [Label 1 Cor 4:6.] He brings forward himself and Apollos, having kept silent the persons of those demanding to be honoured and the disciples to be named from them, so that you may take from us a type and sequence (example) to behave moderately toward the teachers. And do not think beyond what is written about us, but reckon us servants of Christ and stewards of mysteries of God (1 Cor 4:1), and do not dishonour some of the teachers and honour others. More clearly in these he refuted their opinion: for the one named from so-and-so, overlooking so-and-so, was puffed up on behalf of that one, and had the puffing-up against that (other) one. [Label 1 Cor 4:7.] You who wish to be called from this one or to leave that one, who distinguishes (judges) you? Do you not wait for the judge? You the one obeying [page 240] wait for the judge, and do you subject the teacher to your judgement? [Second column, pages 239-240, parallel:] You the layman, who judges you over what you either think or do, that you dare to judge others, and these teachers? Is it not the Lord? If then you the disciple wait for the Lord as judge, how do you subject the teacher to your judgement, calling one worthy and the other unworthy? Why do you think you have an advantage which you neither have nor have received? He means the surpassing intelligence through which it is possible also to judge and test teachers. Even if you received the intelligence from God, one must bring glory to God who gave it, not indeed think great over yourself and be lifted up as putting forward an own advantage. [Label 1 Cor 4:8.] Not that their affairs were so, but he shows that they were so disposed, holding false opinions about themselves, and thought they had been filled with all knowledge so as now to judge even teachers. Already the gifts have become cloying to you and not always longed for. And 'without us' shows: (while) we have not yet reigned, you got ahead to reign; and the 'would that indeed' in between (… continues in the next section).
pass_b_english: …for such boasting is cheap when all things are yours: the apostles (they were sent for the sake of those who would benefit), the world, which came to be for your enjoyment, life, since you are being saved, and death (if death held no terrors, the things of the life to come would not have been preferred to this one). "Things present and things to come" are said on the same principle: those who despise present things as passing obtain the things to come. So all the things he has listed are yours, because you have become Christ's, and those who are made Christ's own are pleasing to God.

The second catena form adds: "All things are yours." How, and in what way? Because you have become Christ's. And to show that those who are made Christ's own are pleasing to God, he added, "and Christ is God's."
On 1 Corinthians 4:1: It is enough for us to be honored as servants of Christ; to have people named after us is offensive.

On 1 Corinthians 4:2: Look on us as servants of God, but do not you inquire which servant is faithful, for that is where your danger lies; and it is not right for teachers to be judged by their pupils. Why does he say this? He was aware that they honored some unworthy teachers and passed over worthy ones, and he foresaw that this would lead to schisms among them. That is why he rebukes them so sharply, hurrying to check the trouble.

On 1 Corinthians 4:3: So that he would not seem to say this out of disdain, as a man who had been slighted, he all but says: Do not think I am sending you this on my own account. I do not live in a way that calls for me to be examined by you. I think that beneath me, where you or any man is concerned. By "a human day" he means human beings, pointing to how passing and short-lived human life is. Then, since "I know nothing against myself" seems a large claim, he added, "but I am not justified by this." For a man can stumble through ignorance without his conscience pricking him. Besides, it is not avoiding evil that justifies; it is achieving virtue that makes a man complete. It is likely, too, that he said this out of restraint: do not think more highly than befits you, but wait for the judge.

On 1 Corinthians 4:5: All the way through he keeps to his aim, bringing to their senses those who wanted to be named after one man and not after another, for that is what people do who sit in judgment on who is worthy and who is not. So do not think more highly than befits you, but wait for the judge. A put-on character can deceive you, but nothing hidden could escape the one who brings to light the hidden things of darkness. He said this because much among them went on by deceit, and unworthy men were honored. Those who were honored were not wholly good; they held to virtue only for show, while those who were good in their nature were passed over. Otherwise he would not have said this.

On 1 Corinthians 4:6: He brings forward himself and Apollos and keeps silent about the names of those who demanded honor and wanted the disciples named after them, so that you may take from us a pattern and an example for treating teachers with moderation. Do not think of us beyond what is written, but regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1), and do not dishonor some teachers while honoring others. Here he exposed their attitude more plainly: whoever was named after one man and slighted another was puffed up on the first man's behalf and turned his conceit against the second.

On 1 Corinthians 4:7: You who want to be called after this man or to drop that one, who judges you? Are you not waiting for the judge? You, whose part is to obey, are waiting for the judge, and yet you put your teacher under your own judgment?

The second catena form adds: And you, a layman, who judges you for what you think or do, that you dare to judge others, and teachers at that? Is it not the Lord? If you, the disciple, wait for the Lord as judge, how can you put your teacher under your own judgment, calling one worthy and another unworthy?

Why do you think you have an advantage that you neither have nor have received? He means the surpassing intelligence that would let a person judge and test even teachers. Even if you received your understanding from God, you must give the glory to God who gave it, not think great things of yourself and be lifted up, putting it forward as an advantage of your own.

On 1 Corinthians 4:8: Not that things really stood so with them; he shows that this was their state of mind. They held false opinions of themselves and thought they had been filled with all knowledge, to the point of judging even their teachers. Already the gifts have become a surfeit to you, and you no longer long for them. "Without us" means: before we reigned, you got there first and reigned. And by setting "would that you did reign" in between…

choices.english: collapsed; new material printed after 'The second catena form adds:'
choices.why: An unmarked second form of the 3:22-23 note repeats 'you have become Christ's ... please God'; only the question 'How, and in what way?' and the link to 'and Christ is God's' are new. ὑφ' ὑμῶν read as the lemma's ὑμῶν.

choices.english: collapsed; new sentences printed after 'The second catena form adds:'
choices.why: Second form of the 4:7 note; 'you, a layman', 'for what you think or do', 'teachers at that', 'Is it not the Lord?', 'calling one worthy and another unworthy' have no counterpart.

choices.english: printed as its own paragraph without a lead-in
choices.why: The edition does not show whether the second column runs on; no attribution boundary is invented.

choices.term: μὴ οὖν φρονεῖτε μείζονα ἢ καθ' ὑμᾶς, ἀλλ' ἀναμένετε τὸν κριτήν (twice)
choices.english: kept in both the 4:3 and the 4:5 notes
choices.why: One sentence shared by two different notes; each note needs it. Not a doublet of a whole note.

choices.term: οὐ τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν φαῦλον δικαιοῖ
choices.english: it is not avoiding evil that justifies
choices.why: Old English 'not failing to do something justifies' lost the negation's object.
